items.title: Bridging Perceptual and Value Signal Evaluation: Meta‐Analytic Evidence for the Claustrum as a Cross‐Domain Integrator in Decision‐Making
items.author: Yumin Liu,  Geng Li,  Yafen Li,  Jialiang Chen,  Huiyu Shi,  Antao Chen
items.content:
Across 90 fMRI studies, ALE and MACM reveal partly specialized fronto-parietal–visual and striato-thalamo-cingulate systems for perceptual and value signal evaluation. Shared convergence in the bilateral claustrum and left medial frontal gyrus highlights candidate cross-domain coordination nodes in decision-making.

Decision-making requires evaluating information across both perceptual and value domains, yet the neural mechanisms supporting this cross-domain convergence remain unclear. Using activation likelihood estimation (ALE) and meta-analytic connectivity modeling (MACM), we conducted a large-scale cross-domain meta-analysis of 90 fMRI studies involving 2564 participants to examine the neural correlates of perceptual and value signal evaluation. The results revealed partially segregated yet overlapping neural architectures for perceptual and value signal evaluation. Perceptual signal evaluation was primarily associated with a dorsal fronto-parietal–visual system, whereas value signal evaluation was mainly associated with a striato-thalamo-cingulate system. Importantly, the conjunction analysis identified the bilateral claustrum and left medial frontal gyrus as shared convergence regions across domains. MACM further showed distinguishable coactivation profiles, suggesting that these shared regions may participate in coordinating domain-specific perceptual and value-related networks rather than forming a single common decision system. Together, these findings support the claustrum as a candidate domain-general integrator that may bridge sensory, motivational, and executive processes, providing a cross-domain account of decision-making.

items.title: Harmonization of Longitudinal Multi‐Scanner Neuroimaging Data With Nonlinear Biological Associations
items.author: Neel M. Desai,  Haochang Shou,  Noah Hillman,  Randa Melhem,  Lori L. Beason‐Held,  Susan M. Resnick,  Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative,  Baltimore Longitudinal Study of Aging,  Christos Davatzikos,  Russell T. Shinohara
items.content:
We develop a ComBat-based approach to harmonize longitudinal multi-source imaging data that can flexibly account for non-linear biological associations of interest. Our method outperforms existing ComBat-based harmonization approaches designed for longitudinal data.

The aggregation of neuroimaging data across multiple sources, typically scanners or imaging sites, has the potential to improve statistical power when conducting inference. The added benefits of increased sample size to inference, however, can be obstructed by unwanted source-specific technical variability that increases difficulty in estimating biological signals of interest. To address this issue, recent methods based on ComBat, a batch-correction procedure originally developed for genomics, have been developed for both cross-sectional and longitudinal neuroimaging data. While these approaches have successfully removed technical batch-specific variability, they restrict their consideration to linear biological associations. In this article we introduce a ComBat-based method to harmonize longitudinal multisource imaging data that can account for nonlinear biological associations of interest. We demonstrate via simulation that, in the presence of nonlinear biological signal, our method outperforms existing ComBat-based approaches designed for longitudinal imaging data, particularly in settings where observed values of relevant biological covariates lack substantial overlap across sources. Using volumetric measurements for 504 subjects combined from both the Baltimore Longitudinal Study of Aging (BLSA) and the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI), we identify the presence of both additive and multiplicative study-specific effects for a substantial number of brain regions and demonstrate the effective removal of their presence on data harmonized by our method. The flexibility of the proposed method towards capturing many types of biological associations makes it a versatile procedure that can be used to harmonize longitudinal biomedical data.

items.title: Unveiling Neuronal Microstructure in the Human Brain In Vivo With Time‐Dependent Radial Diffusivity in a Head‐Only High‐Performance Gradient 3T MRI System
items.author: Ante Zhu,  Jerome J. Maller,  H. Douglas Morris,  Jeffrey P. Guenette,  Flavio Dell’ Acqua,  Chu‐Yu Lee,  Jeffrey McGovern,  Stephan E. Maier,  Raymond Y. Huang,  Andrew L. Alexander,  Maureen N. Hood,  Desmond Teck Beng Yeo,  Steven C. R. Williams,  Carl‐Fredrik Westin,  Vincent B. Ho,  Vincent A. Magnotta,  Hua Li
items.content:
This preliminary study characterized time-dependent radial diffusivity in the human brain in vivo, finding consistently high values in the healthy corticospinal tract. These observations suggest that time-dependent radial diffusivity is sensitive to white matter microstructure associated with large axons, consistent with findings from preclinical studies.

Diffusion time-dependence, defined as variations in diffusivity and/or diffusional kurtosis with diffusion time, has emerged as a valuable non-invasive imaging marker for characterizing tissue microstructural features, such as cell size, density, packing disorder, and membrane permeability. In white matter, diffusion time-dependent changes between the short diffusion time and long diffusion time in radial diffusivity (RD), defined as the diffusivity perpendicular to fiber tracts, were demonstrated to correlate strongly with mean axon diameter in ex vivo spinal cord tissues and to reveal demyelination in mouse corpus callosum. Oscillating gradient spin echo (OGSE) diffusion encoding can sample a high-frequency range of the diffusion spectral density, achieving a short effective diffusion time. Despite its potential to non-invasively unveil neuronal microstructures to improve the assessment and targeted therapy of neurological diseases, OGSE diffusion MRI has only recently become feasible for human in vivo studies with high-performance gradient MRI systems. In this preliminary study, we characterized time-dependent RD with OGSE encoding in the human brain in vivo. The change in radial diffusivity between short diffusion time and long diffusion time (ΔRD) consistently exhibited high values in the corticospinal tract, indicating high sensitivity of ΔRD to large axon diameter in human brains. Imaging at a high OGSE frequency of 100 Hz and a moderate -value of 800 × 10 ms/μm produced the highest ΔRD in the corticospinal tract. This study established a baseline for future investigations of neuronal microstructural alterations in neurological disorders and diseases.

items.title: Brain Stiffness Correlation Networks in Healthy Older Adults Using Magnetic Resonance Elastography
items.author: KowsalyaDevi Pavuluri,  John Huston III,  Richard L. Ehman,  Armando Manduca,  Clifford R. Jack Jr,  Matthew L. Senjem,  David T. Jones,  Yi Sui,  Matthew C. Murphy
items.content:
Using in vivo Magnetic Resonance Elastography, we mapped brain stiffness across 112 gray matter regions in 98 cognitively unimpaired older adults, then built stiffness correlation networks from those regional measurements. The networks show small-world topology ( = 2.44 at 5% density), revealing a systematic biomechanical architecture of the brain.

Magnetic resonance elastography (MRE) quantifies tissue stiffness, a measure of microstructural integrity. While gray matter structural correlation networks are well established, the large-scale topological organization of stiffness correlation networks is not fully characterized. This study introduces the biomechanical covariance network framework, in which stiffness correlation networks reflect inter-individual covariation in regional stiffness across participants after adjusting for age, sex, regional gray matter volume, total intracranial volume, and scanner. We tested whether these networks exhibit small-world topology and how they differ from volume correlation networks. MRE-derived stiffness and MRI-derived gray matter volume maps were analyzed from 98 cognitively unimpaired older adults, and correlation networks of 112 gray matter regions were constructed using the Mayo Clinic Adult Lifespan Template (MCALT) ADIR-122 parcellation. The normalized clustering coefficient (γ$$ \gamma $$), normalized path length, and small-world index (σ$$ \sigma $$) were calculated against degree-preserving null networks across network densities. The stiffness correlation networks exhibited small-world architecture, with high local clustering and short path lengths (σ$$ \sigma $$ = 2.44 at 5% density and above 1 at all densities examined, 5%–51%). Stiffness and volume correlation networks showed partial correspondence ( = 0.306,  < 0.0001) but were not redundant, with the stiffness networks showing stronger local clustering (γ$$ \gamma $$ = 3.01 versus 2.43 at 5% density). These findings establish the biomechanical covariance network framework in cognitively unimpaired older adults and suggest that biomechanical correlations may offer information complementary to volumetric measures. The framework provides a reference for future studies of how these networks change with age, disease, and cognitive decline.

items.title: Variability, but Not Concentration, of Neuromelanin in the Substantia Nigra Is Associated With Individual Differences in Interference Control
items.author: Shuhui Lyu,  Hongchi Zhang,  Jimin Yan,  Jiaqi Gao,  Kangcheng Wang,  Lorenza Colzato,  Bernhard Hommel
items.content:
Differences in neuromelanin signal heterogeneity (NM-SD), not mean levels, predict interference control across sessions, suggesting a stable dopaminergic trait. However, this relationship weakens after accounting for voxel size, implying NM-SD reflects both biological variability and imaging-related factors.

Interference control—the ability to suppress distracting information while selecting task-relevant responses—relies on dopaminergic modulation of fronto-striatal circuits. Although pharmacological evidence shows that transient dopaminergic enhancement can reduce interference, it remains unclear whether stable, trait-like properties of the dopaminergic system constrain individual differences in control efficiency. The present study examined whether the concentration of the neuromelanin signal (NM-Mean), and/or its variability, indexed by the standard deviation of the neuromelanin-sensitive MRI contrast-to-noise ratio (NM-SD), within the substantia nigra is associated with performance in the Flanker conflict task. Sixty healthy young adults completed the task. Neuromelanin CNR maps were registered to MNI152 standard space for ROI definition, and voxel-wise CNR values within the SN–VTA region were extracted in native space to derive NM-Mean and NM-SD. NM-Mean, indexing overall neuromelanin concentration, was not related to behavioral performance. In contrast, lower NM-SD, reflecting more homogeneous dopaminergic integrity, was associated with smaller Flanker interference effects but was unrelated to conflict adaptation across trials. Statistically controlling for voxel size rendered the effect size no longer significant, but a trend remained. These findings provide limited and preliminary evidence that individual differences in dopaminergic signal reliability, rather than overall dopamine quantity, contribute to variability in cognitive control. Although NM-SD is sensitive to acquisition-related factors such as spatial resolution, the observed attenuation of its association with interference control after controlling for voxel size suggests that its behavioral relevance may reflect a mixture of biological variability and methodological influences rather than a clear trait-like property of the dopaminergic system.

items.title: Association of Perivascular Space Volume in Basal Ganglia Subfields With Cognitive Impairment in Cerebral Small Vessel Disease
items.author: Lulu Ai,  Zhiwei Li,  Chaojuan Huang,  Xia Zhou,  Qiaoqiao Xu,  Xiaoqun Zhu,  Zhongwu Sun
items.content:
Schematic overview of the study design and main findings. This cross-sectional single-center study demonstrates that enlarged PVS volume in the basal ganglia (BG) subfields, particularly the caudate and putamen, is associated with worse cognitive function in CSVD. PVS burden increases with age and is more prominent in males, while hippocampal PVS enlargement inversely correlates with hippocampal volume and visuospatial function. These findings highlight regional PVS enlargement as a potential biomarker reflecting age and sex-related glymphatic dysfunction in CSVD.

Perivascular spaces (PVS) serve as essential elements of the glymphatic pathway, facilitating waste clearance and nutrient transport, and their impairment may underlie cognitive deficits in cerebral small vessel disease (CSVD). Here, we investigated associations between PVS characteristics, potential determinants, and cognitive impairment in CSVD. 132 individuals diagnosed with CSVD and 40 healthy controls (HCs) were recruited to participate in a series of thorough neuropsychological assessments and neuroimaging examinations. PVS volume fraction (VF) was quantified in basal ganglia (BG), thalamus, hippocampus, and white matter (WM) using an automated, multimodal image processing pipeline (Enhanced PVS Contrast, EPC) combined with the Frangi filter for robust segmentation. Partial correlation analyses, adjusted for covariates, were performed. CSVD patients exhibited significantly larger PVS VF in the BG and hippocampus, particularly in caudate and putamen subfields of BG (all  < 0.05). In CSVD group, advancing age correlated with elevated PVS VF in both BG and hippocampus, especially in males (all < 0.05). A main effect of sex on PVS VF was observed in this patient cohort across the BG, caudate, hippocampus and thalamus, where males exhibited larger PVS VF than females (all  < 0.05). In HC group, age correlated positively with PVS volume fraction in the BG ( < 0.05), with no significant sex differences across regions. Enlarged BG-PVS was associated with worse global cognitive function (pr = −0.27,  = 0.027) and processing speed (pr = −0.31,  = 0.010), persisting after controlling for other neuroimaging markers (including WMHs, lacunes, and CMBs) and regional volume. Subfield analyses revealed the correlation mainly occurring in the putamen (pr = −0.31,  = 0.010). Hippocampal PVS VF inversely correlated with hippocampal volume (pr = −0.26,  = 0.043), more pronounced in females, and was significantly linked to worse visuospatial function (pr = −0.33,  = 0.010). Regional PVS enlargement in CSVD, particularly in BG and hippocampus regions, reflects underlying glymphatic impairment related to age and sex. The prominence of this finding within BG subregions further underscores their role in the pathogenesis of neurocognitive decline.

items.title: Intrasubject Reconfiguration of the Cortical Gradients' Topological Properties With Cognitive States
items.author: Derek J. Pavelka,  Attakias T. Mertens,  Katrina Myers,  Callum Goldsmith,  Joanna Arch,  Jessica R. Andrews‐Hanna,  Gaelle E. Doucet
items.content:
Cortical gradients' topological properties were computed in 138 healthy young individuals across four fMRI tasks. Our findings suggest the gradients' topological properties are sensitive to different cognitive and attentional demands.

Cortical gradients have been shown to be an effective technique to study the functional organization of the brain by capturing patterns of functional similarities. Until now, most studies have focused on analyzing cortical gradients derived from resting-state fMRI. With recent work highlighting the changes that functional brain networks undergo during various cognitive loads, there is a need to investigate whether cortical gradients are also sensitive to different cognitive demands, and to what degree. In this context, we collected a sample of 138 healthy individuals aged 12–25, each of whom completed a resting-state fMRI scan as well as three task fMRI scans (social prospection, spatial working memory, and verbal working memory). All data were analyzed to examine the task dependence of cortical gradients' topological properties. By employing the measures of network gradient dispersions as well as networks centroid distances, we revealed that alterations specific to each task occurred in topological properties of gradients involving both transmodal and unimodal networks, such as the executive control network varying between each task condition and the resting-state condition. This work highlights the promise of applying cortical gradients to task-based fMRI data, revealing the condition-sensitive nature of certain cortical gradients' topological properties.

items.title: Exposure to Maternal Pre‐ and Postnatal Psychological Distress: Associations With Brain Structure in 5‐Year‐Old Children
items.author: Elmo P. Pulli,  Hilyatushalihah K. Audah,  Amira Svensk,  Eeva Eskola,  Elisabeth Nordenswan,  Aylin Rosberg,  Silja Alvajärvi,  Pauliina Juntunen,  Isabella L. C. Mariani Wigley,  Venla Kumpulainen,  Eero Silver,  Anni Copeland,  Ekaterina Saukko,  Harri Merisaari,  Riikka Korja,  Eeva‐Leena Kataja,  Linnea Karlsson
items.content:
This study provides support for hypotheses proposing that early-life exposure to maternal distress can influence the structural development of the brain. Furthermore, it highlights the role of the early postnatal period and calls for further research into this so far overlooked period and pathways that explain the associations.

Maternal mental health is an important contributor to child neurodevelopment. While there are multiple studies on prenatal exposure, early postnatal exposure has received little attention in neuroimaging research. Five-year-old children ( = 161) were recruited from the FinnBrain Birth Cohort study. Maternal distress was assessed using questionnaires on depressive and anxiety symptoms at 14, 24, and 34 gestational weeks and postnatally at 3, 6, and 24 months. T1-weighted structural images were processed using a voxel-based morphometry pipeline to map associations between maternal distress exposure and regional gray matter (GM) volumes. Whole-brain voxel-wise general linear models were used, accounting for potential confounders. Additionally, a latent class mixed model approach was used to model longitudinal trajectories of distress exposure. We found widespread associations between maternal postpartum distress symptoms and offspring brain morphology. Postnatal distress at 3 months was negatively associated with GM volumes in the left supplementary motor cortex, right cerebellum/fusiform gyrus, and left anterior insula/frontal operculum. Postnatal distress at 6 months was positively associated with GM volumes in the right cuneus and lingual gyrus, right insula/operculum, and right inferior occipital gyrus, while distress at 24 months was negatively associated with GM volumes in the left inferior/middle frontal gyrus. There were no structural brain differences between the latent classes. This study provides support for hypotheses proposing that early-life exposure to maternal distress can influence the structural development of the brain. It highlights the role of the early postnatal period and calls for further research into this so far overlooked period and the developmental pathways that explain these associations.

items.title: SPARK‐ICA: Guided Frequency‐Resolved Dynamic Spatial ICA Reveals Fine‐Scale fMRI Network Dynamics
items.author: N. Behzadfar,  A. Iraji,  V. Calhoun
items.content:
SPARK–ICA is a frequency-resolved dynamic spatial ICA framework that decomposes time-varying fMRI network maps into multiple spatial frequency bands. Applied to schizophrenia resting-state data, it reveals complementary abnormalities in stable connectivity and rapid high-frequency network interactions that are not captured by conventional dynamic connectivity analyses.

Fine-scale spatiotemporal dynamics of functional brain networks are increasingly recognized as critical markers of transient connectivity and neuropsychiatric pathology. However, many existing dynamic fMRI methods primarily focus on temporal variability without explicitly resolving the spatial-frequency content of network dynamics, potentially limiting characterization of subtle, high-frequency spatial reconfigurations. To address this gap, we propose SPARK–ICA (Spatial–frequency Partitioned, Adaptive Reconstruction using Knowledge-guided ICA), a frequency-resolved dynamic spatial independent component analysis (ICA) framework that integrates NeuroMark template guidance with spatial frequency decomposition and group-level ICA of time-resolved, band-specific spatial maps. Starting from template-guided NeuroMark networks, we first estimate time-varying spatial maps using a dynamic guided ICA approach, capturing subject-specific network expression over time. Each dynamic spatial map is then decomposed into multiple spatial frequency bands using Fourier-domain spatial filtering, isolating fine- to coarse-scale spatial features at each time point. Band-specific spatial maps are subsequently concatenated and subjected to a blind group-level multi-frequency ICA, yielding a compact latent representation in which each dynamic component is characterized by distinct spatial-frequency signatures. These group-level band-resolved components are then used as references to estimate subject- and band-specific time courses and maps via spatially constrained ICA, enabling frequency-specific analysis of both long-term correlations and short-term temporal variability while preserving reproducibility across subjects. Using resting-state fMRI data from schizophrenia (SZ) patients and healthy controls (HC), we evaluated both long-term correlations and short-term variability of band-resolved dynamic time courses. For the group-level analyses, we focused on a predefined subset of NeuroMark networks with well-established involvement in SZ-related dysconnectivity. Our results reveal frequency-specific abnormalities in SZ, with enhanced long-term connectivity within sensory and subcortical networks and pronounced short-term alterations involving predominantly higher-frequency spatial components, particularly in cerebellar and subcortical systems. These findings indicate that SZ-related dysregulation is differentially expressed across spatial-frequency and temporal scales, rather than reflecting uniform dysconnectivity. Together, this framework provides a unified approach for analyzing dynamic fMRI networks across spatial, temporal, and frequency dimensions, extending our previous NeuroMark-DyFICA framework from a predominantly high-frequency spatial representation to an explicitly frequency-resolved characterization of dynamic network organization. By explicitly modeling spatial frequency–dependent dynamics, the proposed method provides a more resolved characterization of network alterations and offers a framework for identifying candidate markers of neuropsychiatric disorders.

items.title: Functional Network Organization Underlying Individual Differences in False Feedback Susceptibility: A Graph Theoretical Analysis
items.author: J. Patchitt,  T. Karapanagiotidis,  S. N. Garfinkel,  M. Miller,  M. Tsakiris,  A. Clark,  H. D. Critchley
items.content:
Individual differences in susceptibility to somatosensory false feedback (sFFB) predict altered network topography between regions previously implicated in sFFB. This work supports an interoceptive integration model of sFFB and highlights the importance of network topology in determining how individuals weigh and integrate internal and external physiological information during emotional processing.

Individual differences in susceptibility to somatosensory false physiological feedback reflect variations in interoceptive processing, yet the underlying neural network mechanisms remain unclear. We analyzed resting-state functional connectivity using graph theoretical approaches in 41 healthy adults who completed a somatosensory false feedback paradigm. Nine regions of interest were defined from previous activation analyses, and network topology metrics including local efficiency, clustering coefficient, centrality measures, and path length were calculated across multiple thresholds. Three distinct patterns of network organization predicted false feedback susceptibility. Individuals more susceptible to false feedback showed: (1) increased posterior insula eccentricity, indicating network peripheralization of this key interoceptive region; (2) consistent orbitofrontal cortex segregation across multiple metrics including increased path length and decreased centrality measures; and (3) cerebellar network reconfiguration with reduced local efficiency but increased betweenness centrality. Somatosensory false feedback susceptibility reflects specific alterations in functional network topology, particularly reduced integration of interoceptive regions (posterior insula) and emotional appraisal systems (orbitofrontal cortex). These findings support a network-based model where interoceptive processing depends on efficient integration between visceral sensation, emotional evaluation, and cognitive control systems. Understanding these network properties may inform interventions targeting interoceptive awareness and emotional regulation.
